walkthroughs.body_html:
Human Geography: Population — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Human Geography: Population brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Human Geography: Population.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the replacement fertility rate?

options: Malthus
Boserup
Ehrlich
Rostow

mcqs.q: Does a falling birth rate immediately stop population growth?
options: No — population momentum means a youthful age structure keeps growth going for decades, as large cohorts reach childbearing age even at lower fertility.
Populations only grow in leap years.
Once fertility falls to replacement level, the population stops growing straight away.
Overpopulation is measured by counting cars.

mcqs.q: Was Malthus right that population always outruns food supply?
options: Malthusian famine checks have operated exactly as predicted.
Overpopulation is measured by counting cars.
Malthus invented modern fertiliser.
His prediction has not held so far — technology, the Green Revolution and trade raised food output faster than he foresaw, as Boserup argued, though resource limits remain debated.

mcqs.q: Is overpopulation simply about high population density?
options: Populations only grow in leap years.
Overpopulation is measured by counting cars.
Crowded places are by definition overpopulated.
No — overpopulation is when population exceeds carrying capacity given current resources and technology; a dense, wealthy area can be well supported while a sparse, arid one is overpopulated.
